newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway central bank under pressure to cut rates.
newsitem.headline: Norway central bank under pressure to cut rates.

text.p: Norway's central bank, anxious not to fuel inflation, is trying to resist market expectations that the strong crown could soon trigger an official interest rate cut, analysts say.

The crown has been firming for months because the economy is strong and foreign investors have been buying Norwegian currency due to short term money market rates which have been markedly higher than their German equivalent.

"The crown is appreciating more than the central bank wants it to," said Eirik Larsen, a senior currency analyst with Den norske Bank (DnB). "This helps increase expectations of an official interest rate cut."

The primary objective of Norwegian monetary policy is exchange rate stability, but the central bank is worried about cutting rates because this could drive up inflation and overheat the oil-rich country's booming economy.
Instead, the bank sold more than 86 billion crowns in 1996 to counter appreciation pressures on the undervalued currency, which has reached its strongest levels since 1992.
Analysts were unsure when the bank might cave in and cut the overnight deposit rate and the overnight lending rate charged to commercial and savings banks.
They were both cut by 0.5 percentage points on November 6 last year to 4.0 and 6.0 percent respectively, but the runaway crown has not been reined in.

"The crown will continue to firm, the central bank will keep intervening and in the end they will have to cut the rates," Oeystein Stephansen, a senior bond analyst with S-E Banken in Oslo, told Reuters. "It is difficult to say when, but it could happen sooner than many think and before the end of February."
Larsen said: "I cannot say the cuts will happen today or next week. They could come any moment. There is pressure in the market, which has already discounted for a 50 basis point cut.
"If Norwegian short rates come down to German levels it would dampen demand for Norwegian crowns because investors could stick to the German rates," Larsen said.
Norwegian three-month eurokrone swap rates were down eight basis points at 3.55 percent on Tuesday afternoon, narrowing the gap to the German three-month rate to less than 40 basis points.
Leif Eide, chief of market operations at the central bank, said the bank's currency policy was no reason why Norwegian money market rates could not fall below the German equivalents.
"The central bank's policy of currency stability is no reason why German rates should form the floor for Norwegian money market rates," Eide told Reuters.
"If money market rates are to be below German ones, then official interest rates must be reduced," Eide added, but he would not speculate whether official rates would be cut.
The central bank's 4.0 rate on overnight deposits normally sets the floor for money market rates, but now commercial banks can borrow money from each other at rates below the benchmark.
